The present collection has been brought to print by the highest **Electoral** <note>Refers to the Prince-Elector of Bavaria, Karl Theodor (reigned 1777–1799), who issued the edicts banning the Illuminati.</note> command in order to all the more convince the public, both at home and abroad, of the obvious **groundlessness** <note>original: "Ungrund." It serves further to warn the public against this **epidemic sect**, as well as all other similar forbidden **clandestine societies** <term>original: "Winkelgesellschaften." Literally "corner-societies," a derogatory term used by the authorities to describe secret groups that met in private to avoid state supervision.</term> in which people seek only to deceive the **gullible**, to **fleece** <note>original: "schneuzen." A colloquial term for swindling or "cleaning out" someone's finances.</note> them of their money, and where—instead of the feigned **enlightenment of truth** and **improvement of morals**—the effort is rather to fundamentally corrupt the latter and to entirely suppress or falsify the former.

Who <meta>catchword: Wer</meta>

# Revision
## of the Illuminati Order.

Under this title, a work will shortly appear at the Strobl Bookstore <note>The Stroblische Buchhandlung in Munich was a prominent publisher used by the Bavarian government to disseminate anti-Illuminati literature and official decrees during the late 1780s.</note> in Munich, which will exhaustively treat and perhaps entirely settle this subject, which has been so dark and complicated until now; for only now, following the publication of the original Illuminati writings released by supreme command <note>Referring to the Elector Karl Theodor’s order to publish the seized papers of the Order to turn public opinion against them.</note>, can this be done in a manner that satisfies the public.

The work carries the motto: **Tear apart the chain, but spare the useful links!** — Equally distant from personal considerations and blind partisan rage, it will investigate, explain, and prove what is still hidden, doubtful, and unproven. It will deal with matters, not persons.

Its contents are:

I. On the mysteries of the ancients. A parallel between ancient and modern mysteries.

II. Should a state tolerate secret societies?

III. Regarding Illuminatism <term>original: "Illuminatismus." A contemporary term used to describe the system, philosophy, and collective activities of the Order of the Illuminati.</term> in Bavaria in particular.

IV. Its origin, its flowering, and its fall.

<summary>This page announces a forthcoming book titled "Revision of the Illuminati Order," which aims to provide a factual, objective history of the secret society using newly available state-published evidence.</summary>
<keywords>Revision, Illuminati Order, Strobl Bookstore, Munich, secret societies, Bavaria, ancient mysteries, legal tolerance</keywords>

--- Page 12 ---
<meta>This page continues the announcement of the "Revision of the Illuminati Order," emphasizing the work's comprehensive nature and its relationship to the official government-published seized documents.</meta>

All pamphlets that have appeared over the last three years concerning this rightly notorious matter <note>The "notorious matter" refers to the scandal and subsequent legal suppression of the Order of the Illuminati in Bavaria, which began in 1784 and culminated in the publication of their secret papers.</note>, excluding those of no consequence, are cited according to their essential content in this work. In this way, the domestic and foreign reader will finally receive the long-desired and complete instruction on the subject.

The recently published original Illuminati writings <note>original: "illuminatische Originalschriften." These were the primary source documents seized from the homes of prominent members like Xavier von Zwack, which the Bavarian government published in 1787 to justify their crackdown on the secret society.</note> are to be considered as a second volume containing the supplements to the work announced here; for the majority of the public, one would be an incomplete work without the other.

->Munich, April 6, 1787.<-

<summary>This page concludes the publisher's announcement for a definitive history of the Illuminati, framing it as an essential companion to the official government-released documents for a complete understanding of the controversy.</summary>

### Note.

Those words printed in Schwabacher type <term>Schwabacher: A bold, cursive style of German blackletter typography used here to represent emphasis or specific formatting in the original source documents.</term> are underlined in the original documents. Anything appearing in small print <note>original: "Petites Lettres" (French). The editor uses a smaller font size to differentiate their own commentary from the primary text.</note> is an addition or a remark.

Where a dash ( — ) appears in the text, a word has been omitted; and the hyphens ( = ) indicate the specific number of syllables in the missing words.

The three tables cited on pages 163 and 361 can be found at the end of the volume.

**Vocabulary:** Note, Schwabacher type, Small print, Text, Tables

## 2. Establishment of the Women's Order.

->In Zwack's handwriting.<-

This must consist of two classes, each of which constitutes a separate society, and each must remain unknown to the other because of their connection <note>original: "Nexus"</note>.

One class of the virtuous, the other of the debauched <note>original: *Ausschweifenden*, referring to those living an unrestrained or decadent lifestyle</note>. It must be unknown to both that they are guided by the men's order, and the superior of each class must believe she has a Grand Lodge from which she receives orders; which, however, are fundamentally given by the men. Both classes must [be guided] through instruction—both mutual and through proposed male teachers, who would be members of the Order <note>the original uses the symbol ☉ to denote the Order</note>, but would remain unknown to themselves and to [the women]. [This is to be achieved] through the delivery of good books, and for the latter class, through the secret gratification of their passions.

During the search of Zwack’s house <note>original: "Hausvisitation"</note>, [these notes] were found on two octavo sheets <note>a book or paper size resulting from folding a sheet of paper to create eight leaves</note>.

# VI.

## Statutes of the Illuminati.

Since the Society does not intend to abolish those rational bonds by which one is attached to the State, but rather to strengthen them further, it is their will:

1. That all shall be met with love, respect, distinction, and according to their social standing.

2. Therefore, everyone shall at all times remain within the bounds of ceremony <term>Ceremoniel: the formal etiquette and protocol governing social interactions in the 18th century</term>, especially when members are among non-initiates <term>Profanen: literally "the profane"; those who have not been initiated into the secrets of the Order</term>; thus, every distinguished nobleman (even if he holds a lower rank within the Order) shall be shown the proper respect due to his status. And because it is important to us that our members are honored by non-initiates, they shall receive even greater honor from our own people, so that others may likewise hold them in high esteem.

3. Among the Order’s brothers alone, however, all distinctions of rank held in civil society disappear, and only the seniority and character <term>Karakter: the specific grade or rank one has achieved within the Illuminati’s internal system, regardless of their job or title in the outside world</term> one holds within the Order shall apply. There, everyone—even the most humble senior member, and even more so the superiors—shall be met with the same reverence as one would meet a person of high standing among non-initiates— <note>The text breaks off here; the catchword "de" indicates the word would have been "würde," meaning "would [be met with]."</note>

### VI.

## Statutes of the Illuminati.

Since the society does not intend to abolish the reasonable bonds to which one is bound in the state, but rather to strengthen them, its will is:

1. That everyone be met with love, respect, distinction, and according to their social standing.

2. Therefore, everyone should at all times remain within the bounds of ceremony; even more so when members find themselves among the profane <term>Profanen: "the profane," a term common in secret societies for the uninitiated public who remain "outside the temple"</term>. Thus, every distinguished nobleman (even if he were of lower rank within the Order) should be shown the proper and status-appropriate respect; and because it is important to us that our members be honored by the profane, they should receive even greater honor from our own people, so that others might also hold them in high esteem.

3. However, among the brothers of the Order alone, all differences of social status held in civil society <term>bürgerliche Gesellschaft: the public, legal, and professional sphere of the state</term> disappear, and only the seniority and character one possesses within the Order shall count. There, every elder, even the humblest, and even more so the superiors, shall be met with the same reverence as one would meet high-ranking persons among the profane,

### VII.

## Reform of the Statutes
## of the 1st Class.

Since legislative wisdom requires that, following a change in circumstances, the necessary regulations and laws must also be altered—to prevent, through new laws, those abuses that have crept in over time, to clarify doubtful cases more closely, and to make specific decrees issued in the meantime general and incorporate them into the regular book of laws when necessary—the Order has made the following provisions in regard to the First Class during its last general assembly.

Whether he has properly considered that he is taking a major step here, and is undertaking unknown obligations <term>Verbindlichkeiten</term>? <note>The "unknown obligations" refer to the candidate's pledge of secrecy and obedience even before they were fully informed of the Order's higher-level goals.</note>

3. For what reasons is he entering the Order? What does he hope and expect to find within it?

4. Whether he would still enter the Order if it had no other ultimate purpose than moral perfection <term>moralische Vollkommenheit</term>, and no other advantages? <note>"Moral perfection" was a central Enlightenment ideal; Weishaupt taught that if individuals became perfectly self-governed through reason, external government and the "rule of princes" would eventually become unnecessary.</note>

5. What if the Order were new, had few members, or were merely an invention of the recruiter <term>Aufnehmer</term>? <note>This question tested whether the candidate was joining for the sake of the Order's principles or merely for the prestige of an established, powerful organization.</note>

6. What if improper or unjust things were to occur within it?

7. Whether he can consider the welfare of the Order as his own?

8. Whether he is willing to love all members?

9. Even if he were to find his enemies among them?

10. Whether he would even—if it were necessary and it depended on him—do good to his enemies, recommend them, and praise them? <note>This reflects the Order's emphasis on cosmopolitanism and the "universal love of mankind," aiming to rise above personal grievances for the greater good of the association.</note>

11. Whether in his absence he would still wish to involve himself with the members of the Order?

# XV.

## Ceremonies and Solemnities
->at the <term>Initiation</term><- <note>original: "Initiation"</note>

The act of <term>initiation</term> <note>original: "Einweihung"</note> always takes place by day in a solitary, secluded, and somewhat dark place—for example, a forest—or at night in a quiet, secluded room at a time when the moon is in the sky. The room must be as dark as possible; in two corners, a table with an oil lamp is to be placed. At one table sits the <term>initiator</term> <note>original: "Einweihende"</note>, and at the other, the <term>initiate</term> <note>original: "Einzuweihende"</note>. The lamp must burn dimly and only shine upon the person who requires it for reading. No one else is present except for the initiate and the one who is admitting him.

After the preceding oath has been taken, the aspiring Candidate is addressed as follows:

1. That in this upcoming class, he is still free to withdraw; however, the obligation of **secrecy** <note>original: "Stillschweigen"; a core requirement of secret societies to ensure the group's security and prevent the exposure of members</note> binds him even more strongly than before.

2. Should he err in believing that he will presently become acquainted with all members of the **Order**, these members have the highest reason to remain hidden from him for now; in due time, he himself will approve of this caution. However, means will be provided to him to discover some through his own effort. (At this point, the **signs** <note>original: "Zeichen"; secret gestures, handshakes, or symbols used for recognition between members without alerting outsiders</note> are taught to him.)

3. He shall, within the space of a month (if he desires a longer time, it is at his discretion), submit a **catalog** <note>original: "Verzeichniß"; the Order monitored the intellectual leanings of its members by reviewing their personal libraries</note> of his books, including those of legal scholars, theologians, **ascetics** <note>religious practitioners who practice self-denial and spiritual discipline</note>, preachers, schoolbooks, philosophers, **chemists** <note>original: "Chimisten"; in the 18th century, this often encompassed both scientific chemistry and the older traditions of alchemy</note>, etc. etc. The catalog must be divided into sections, and the edition of each book must be noted.

4. No less shall he, within this same timeframe, draft and hand in his thoughts on the following items:

1) What he desires the **ultimate purpose** <note>original: "Endzweck"; the final goal or mission</note> of the Order to be.

2) What means he would employ to achieve this purpose.

3) What organizational structure he would establish if he were tasked with founding an **Order** <note>a secret society or fraternal organization, likely modeled on the Freemasons or Illuminati</note>.

4) What things he specifically wishes *not* to occur or be found within the Order.

5) Which types of people he hopes *not* to encounter within it.

Should it happen, however, that the **Candidate** <note>original: "Candidat"; the aspirant undergoing the initiation process</note> wishes to withdraw from his intention, either during the proceedings themselves or at their conclusion, he is by no means to be detained. Instead, after being commanded to maintain the strictest **secrecy** <note>original: "Stillschweigen"; the fundamental rule of silence regarding the group's existence and activities</note>, he is to be dismissed with all courtesy.

If the **Initiate** <note>original: "Recipiendus"; the one being received into the order</note> presents doubts to his **Initiator** <note>original: "Recipienten"; the higher-ranking member conducting the reception</note> that the latter is unable to answer **immediately** <note>original Latin: "in continenti"; on the spot or without delay</note>, the proceedings shall be suspended until further notice, or continued as circumstances permit, with the answers to the questions and doubts deferred until instruction is received from superiors. However, if the ceremony is to be interrupted, the doubts and concerns raised must be of a very significant nature.

## *The Profession of Faith.* <note>original French: "La Profession de foi"</note>

->In Zwack’s handwriting.<- <note>referring to Franz Xaver von Zwack, a prominent early member and high-ranking official of the Illuminati</note>

I, [Name], hereby confess in this present place and in the presence of this member of the illustrious **Society** <note>original: "Gesellschaft"; referring to the Order</note>, into which, after mature reflection and having completed the **probationary period** <note>original: "Probezeit"; the time during which a candidate's character was observed</note>, I most longingly desire to be admitted; and I pledge to the same that during this time I have sufficiently experienced, perceived, and reflected that I came from the hands of **Nature** <note>a central concept in Enlightenment thought, emphasizing man's natural state over social artifice</note>, from my mother's womb, poor, helpless, and without rank or honors; that these my goods, fortune, and status are acquired things; that insofar as I received them from my ancestors without any action of my own, I have no reason to be proud; that without the assistance of my **fellow human beings** <note>original: "Nebenmenschen"; a term emphasizing social interconnectedness</note> and parents, I could never have reached this age and degree; and that I am fully grateful to all who contributed to this, and will serve them in return according to my strength and opportunity. No less do I confess that I have seen from this that the approval and help of my fellow human beings is important and necessary to me; that without such I am nothing; that I love them for this reason; and that I am ready to serve them, and by virtue

## XX.
## Thoughts
### on
# Suicide.

->From the handwriting of Zwack.<- <note>Referring to Franz Xaver von Zwack, whose Order name was "Cato." He was a central figure in the Illuminati and a legal counselor in Munich.</note>

To lift the curtain and step behind it, that is all; and why the hesitation and trembling? Is it because we do not know what it looks like back there, and because no one returns? — It is the nature of our spirit to sense confusion and darkness in those things about which we know nothing definite.

Even the mere thought of suicide <term>self-murder|original: Selbstmord</term> <note>The 18th-century German term "Selbstmord" carries a heavier moral and legal weight than the modern "suicide," literally meaning "self-murder."</note> arouses revulsion. — Yet, depending on how one views it, and for what reasons one considers it, does a martyr’s death, or a fanatical <note>original: "phantastische," which in this context implies a delusional or overly imaginative obsession.</note> inclination toward penance, arouse any less revulsion in the eyes of rational philanthropy? <note>original: "Menschenliebe," a core Enlightenment value meaning "love of humanity" or benevolence.</note>

Why is it that, in order to speak of a matter, one must always immediately declare: this is good, this is evil, this is foolish, this is wise! What is the meaning of all this? Have you humans, for that reason, investigated the inner relationships of an action? Do you know how to determine with certainty the causes of why it happened,

why it had to happen? If you had done that, you would not be so hasty with your judgments.

The objection—that certain actions remain vicious <note>original: "lasterhaft," meaning full of vice or morally depraved.</note> regardless of the motive behind them—is not so significant; for tell me: theft is a vice, but does the man who resorts to robbery to save himself and his family from a shameful death by starvation deserve compassion or punishment? <meta>This page continues the argument from page 112, completing the analogy of a person driven by the terror of a fire. It transitions into a philosophical defense of suicide, framing it as a psychological "sickness unto death" rather than a moral failing or act of cowardice.</meta>

...feels his nerves strained together, and carries away loads with ease which he could hardly move in a calm state of mind; one who, in the fury of an insult, takes on six others and overpowers them—are these to be called weak? If exertion is strength, why should over-tension <note>original: "Ueberspannung," referring to a state of being over-strained or hyper-excited, often used in this period to describe emotional or mental instability.</note> be the opposite? — Human nature has its limits; it can endure sorrow, joy, and pain up to a certain degree, and it perishes as soon as that degree is exceeded. The question of whether one is weak or strong does not belong here; rather, the question is whether he can endure the measure of his suffering, whether it be moral or physical. I find it just as strange <note>original: "wunderbar," which in the 18th century often meant "strange," "surprising," or "marvelous" rather than "wonderful" in the modern sense.</note> to say that the man who takes his own life is a coward, as it would be improper to call someone a coward who dies of a malignant fever. 

One calls it a sickness unto death <note>original: "Krankheit zum Tode." This phrase famously describes a despair so deep it leads to the destruction of the self.</note> when nature is so attacked that its powers are partly consumed, and partly so incapacitated that it is unable to help itself up again, or to restore the usual circulation of life through any fortunate revolution <note>In a medical context, a "revolution" refers to a sudden, decisive change in the course of a disease, like a crisis that leads to recovery.</note>. Now, applying this to the mind: let us consider man in his limited state, how impressions work upon him, how ideas fix themselves in his mind, until finally a growing passion robs him of all calm mental power <term>Sinneskraft|The faculty of rational perception and steady judgment</term> and utterly ruins him. In vain does the composed, rational man...

<summary>The author argues that suicide is not an act of cowardice but a result of human nature reaching its breaking point, comparable to a terminal physical illness. ->In Zwackh's hand; and signature.<-

->Munich, October 30, 1777.<-

Dearest Friend!

It is better for me that I go; farewell. Convince yourself of my honesty, and convince others of it as well.

Defend my death; strengthen the honest and modest thinkers in the good judgment they will form of it; have pity on the rest of the critics. Remain upright, remember me, and remind my few good friends of this as well. Do not mourn me, farewell! For eternity, I tell you that I am your true friend,

Arrange everything else enclosed here. The ring is a small keepsake for you.

In every well-ordered society, there must exist superiors and subordinates—those with mastery of the whole and laypeople <term>Idioten: derived from the Greek *idiōtēs*, referring here to private persons or those without specialized leadership training, rather than a lack of intelligence</term>—in greater or smaller numbers, determined by specific years of service and merit. Anyone who knows that it is the duty of a society's superiors to provide regulations for the subordinates will naturally conclude that the conduct of the subordinates must align with that of their superiors—or at least with their guidance—and that both good order and disorder are always to be attributed to the latter. Thus, almost every action of those who obey that proves harmful to the whole can be traced back either to the malice, the confusion, or the culpable negligence of those who command.

### On the Behavior of Superiors among Themselves.

The influence that this conduct has upon the whole organization is too well-known for me to dwell long on the proof of it. All actions of the heads of a society are scrutinized with an eager eye by the **subordinates** (see the *Social System* <note>original: "Systéme Social." This likely refers to Baron d'Holbach’s 1773 work *Système Social*, which argued that morality should be based on social utility rather than religion.</note>), and because the **spirit of imitation** <note>A common Enlightenment-era psychological concept suggesting that humans naturally model their behavior after those they perceive as successful or high-status.</note> only follows those whom one believes to be happy, they are chosen by most as models according to which they wish to form and conduct themselves. 

If, therefore, anything improper or contrary to the law is present in their behavior, they draw contempt, mockery, and hatred from the wiser portion of the membership; furthermore, for the less modest member—who assumes the greatness of a person's spirit follows from the loftiness of their rank—they provide an opportunity to awaken the very same **disagreements** among themselves by following and imitating this adverse behavior, which had previously arisen among the superiors for that very same reason.

### Spartacus to Ajax. <note>original: "Ajaci" — the Latin dative case meaning "to Ajax."</note>

I do not know why I hear nothing more at all of our cause? If perhaps regret is setting in, or if they have lost interest in it, then have the goodness to write to me, as I still have time to let our undertaking <note>original: "Unternehmen"</note> drop. It is no great art to make a great resolution; but to defy time, to endure and hold out in what one has conceived on a grand scale, and to execute it with greatness and steadfastness—that is where the great spirit reveals itself, and where many great projects <note>original: "Projecte"</note> have failed. — What is Livius doing? Do this, my Lucilius! Claim yourself for yourself, and the time that until now was being taken away, or stolen, or was slipping away, collect and save it. Persuade yourself that it is as I write: some moments are snatched from us, some are withdrawn, and some simply flow away. However, the most shameful loss is that which occurs through negligence. If you are willing to pay attention, you will see that a great part of life elapses for those who act badly, the greatest part for those who do nothing, and the whole of life for those who are occupied with things that do not matter. Who can you show me who places any value on time, or who estimates the worth of a single day? — Therefore, do this, my Lucilius! Embrace every hour; thus it will happen that you depend less on tomorrow, provided you lay a hand on today. While life is being postponed, it rushes past. All things, Lucilius, belong to others; only time is our own. <note>original: "Ita fac, mi Lucili! vindica te tibi..." from Seneca’s *Moral Letters to Lucilius*, Letter 1. This passage emphasizes the Illuminati’s focus on self-mastery and the productive use of time.</note>

->*Seneca, Letter 1.*<-

You will never bring back the same character you took out with you. The company of the masses is harmful. There is no one who does not either recommend some vice to us, or impress it upon us, or smear it on us without our knowing. Certainly, the larger the crowd with which we mingle, the greater the danger. <note>original: "Nunquam mores, quos effers, referes..." from Seneca’s *Moral Letters to Lucilius*, Letter 7. This reflects the Order's elitist view that the "common" public could corrupt the budding virtue of an initiate.</note>

->*Seneca, Letter 7.*<-

Nothing more effectively clothes the mind in honor, and recalls those who are doubtful and inclined toward depravity back to the right path, than the company of good men. For it gradually sinks into the heart, <note>original: "Nulla res magis animis honesta induit..." from Seneca’s *Moral Letters to Lucilius*, Letter 94. Weishaupt used such passages to justify the "secret" association of the Order as a necessary environment for moral perfection.</note>

...proceed other than slowly. Only deeds, not recommendations, can carry weight here.

In the next class, I am thinking, therefore, of establishing a kind of learned academy: in such a place, work will be done on characters—both historical and living—the study of the ancients, the spirit of observation, treatises, and prize questions. Specifically <note>original: "in specie"</note>, I will turn everyone within it into a spy for one another, and for everyone else. Following this, those who are capable will be selected for the mysteries, which in this class consist of several principles and fundamental requirements for a happy human life. Alongside this, work is done on the recognition and exposure of prejudices. Each member must report these—for example <note>original: "v. g." or "verbi gratia"</note>, monthly—noting which ones he discovers within himself? Which is the dominant one? How far has he come in overcoming them? For us, this is exactly what confession was for the Jesuits. In this highest council <note>original: "Conseil"</note>, projects are drafted regarding how to gradually confront the enemies of reason and humanity: how to initiate the matter among the members of the <term>Sun</term> <note>The symbol ☉ represents the Order of the Illuminati.</note>, and to whom it should be entrusted?

Just as everyone can be employed according to the proportion <note>original: "a proportione"</note> of their insight; I will handle education and other subjects in the same way.

March 10, 1778.

->Spartacus sends greetings to Cato.<- <note>original: "Spartacus Catoni S. d."; S. d. is an abbreviation for the Latin "Salutem dicit," a traditional greeting. Spartacus is the pseudonym of Adam Weishaupt, and Cato is the pseudonym of Xavier von Zwack.</note>

1. The four locations—Athens <note>Munich</note>, Sparta <note>Erlangen</note>, Thebes <note>Freising</note>, and Erzerum <note>Ingolstadt</note>—are only to look after their own local affairs. Regarding my future residence, I can as of yet write nothing definite to you. For the time being I am living in Nuremberg, and will remain there for about 14 days. I am lodging at the Red Rooster; however, I am sometimes in Erlangen, sometimes in Altdorf, and now live quietly and safely. I am also making various good <term>acquaintances</term> <note>original: "Connoissancen". In the 18th-century context, this implies building a network of social and intellectual support.</note>. When the weather becomes milder and I receive an answer to my letter, I shall move further. I want to see what men will do for me, after I have done so much for them. But no, I did not act for the sake of reward.

Friend! A time will surely come when people will wish us back and allow justice to prevail. Simply see to it that, in the meantime, our enemies are not further provoked. But as for us, it is unlikely we shall see each other again; for I intend never to return, even under the most advantageous conditions. Give my regards to <term>Marius</term> <note>Pseudonym for Count Sandizell.</note>, <term>Diomedes</term> <note>Pseudonym for the Marquis de Constanza, one of Weishaupt's most active recruiters.</note>, and
